source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight, JEP:LMC 29(5):1017-1027
finding: Jones put representational change theory (RCT) and progress monitoring theory (PMT) head to head on an unlimited-move problem to which neither had been applied. Both got support. His manipulations of the problem pointed to RCT as the better indicator of performance. He also argued that eye-movement data are a good way to test insight theories.
numbers: Abstract read only (Europe PMC). Full text was blocked this session (HTTP 403 or redirect). No solution rates, N or statistics were seen. The exact task is not named in the abstract.
quote: These 2 theories are tested in an unlimited move problem, to which neither theory has previously been applied.
limits: Abstract only. 'Better indicator' is a relative claim inside one task. Later papers cite the same study as support for both theories (see a11).
agent_relevance: Evidence weight for choosing triggers: neither theory won outright. Use a knowledge trigger (reframe the representation) and a progress trigger (criterion failure), not one alone.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod & Chronicle (2001) Information processing and insight: a process model of performance on the nine-dot and related problems, JEP:LMC 27(1):176-201
finding: Founding paper of progress monitoring (later called Criterion for Satisfactory Progress, CSP). The model uses two heuristics: maximising (take the move that cancels most dots) and progress monitoring with some lookahead. These heuristics cause the difficulty, and they also set up the search for insightful moves once the progress check fails. Five experiments; Expts 4 and 5 compared the model with earlier theories.
numbers: Abstract read only. Numbers for Expts 4-5 come from a second-hand source (a11).
limits: Abstract only. Knowledge-lean spatial problems. Hand-specified model.
agent_relevance: The agent's impasse detector is close to CSP criterion failure: change strategy when no available move meets a progress criterion (for example remaining items divided by remaining budget). Supports G1.

source: Ormerod, MacGregor & Chronicle (2002) Dynamics and constraints in insight problem solving, JEP:LMC 28(4):791-799
finding: Two experiments on the 8-coin problem. Strategic moves that look like progress but guarantee failure lowered solution rates (Expt 1). When such moves were available, people used visual hints to the correct first move less (Expt 2). The authors say insight needs a dynamic that steers search toward the constraints, not only the constraints. Per a11, solutions to this problem were reproducible months later even when only shown.
numbers: Abstract read only; no counts seen.
limits: Abstract only. One problem.
agent_relevance: Misleading progress cues can beat a correct hint. If the agent gets a hint or tool output, a greedy score may override it. Check hints against the progress criterion.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor & Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? The roles of heuristics, goal conception, and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems, JEP:LMC 30(1):14-27
finding: Four experiments on 6-coin and 10-coin problems. Solvers follow a hill-climbing (maximising) heuristic. The difficulty is conceptual, not procedural. The same move-selection rules apply to both problems. Post-solution recoding may explain part of the felt insight.
numbers: Abstract read only. Per a11, 6-coin solution rates were under 20%.
quote: hill-climbing heuristics provide a common framework for understanding transformation and insight problem solving.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Hill-climbing is the default failure of any scaffold with a numeric score. A trigger must be allowed to choose a move that lowers the score.

source: Kershaw & Ohlsson (2004) Multiple causes of difficulty in insight: the case of the nine-dot problem, JEP:LMC 30(1):3-13
finding: One problem is hard for several reasons at once (perception, prior knowledge, process), so removing one cause gives small gains. Three nine-dot experiments support this multiple-factors view and revise the classic explanation.
numbers: Abstract read only; no numbers seen.
limits: Abstract only. Later papers cite it as showing that both knowledge and strategy matter (a11, a08).
agent_relevance: Explains why theory-comparison studies often end with 'both'. Stack triggers (reframe, widen the move set, hint) and test each at equal tokens (G7).

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving, CogSci 42 - Experiment 1 (chunk tightness x numerical value)
finding: Direct RCT vs CSP test with matchstick algebra. RCT predicts loose-chunk problems are solved more than tight-chunk ones. CSP predicts large-value equations are solved more, because a big number disparity cues the right move. Both effects appeared, and the value effect almost erased the chunk effect.
numbers: N=121 after exclusions (129 recruited). Solved in 5 min: low value loose 23/30 (77%); low value tight 13/30 (43%); high value loose 28/31 (90%); high value tight 24/31 (77%). Logistic model chi2(3)=21.6, p=.001; Chunking Wald=8.12 p=.004; Value Wald=8.65 p=.003; interaction ns. First moves on loose chunks: low value 93% vs 76%; high value 63% vs 52%.
limits: Students at open days. One problem per cell, 5-minute limit, between subjects. Authors are CSP proponents.
agent_relevance: Both knowledge structure and progress cues change success. A cheap code-computed disparity signal can stand in for knowledge relaxation.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving, CogSci 42 - Experiment 2 (tautology x value)
finding: Standard tautology (the hardest class in Knoblich 1999) vs reverse tautology (the tautology is already shown; RCT says easier). Reverse was easier, as RCT predicts. But a high-value disparity lifted the standard tautology almost to the reverse rate, as CSP predicts.
numbers: N=133 after exclusions (144 recruited). Standard tautology: low value 4/32 (12%); high value 21/34 (62%). Reverse tautology: low 23/32 (72%); high 28/35 (77%). Model chi2(3)=39.30, p<.001; Tautology Wald=19.33 p<.001; Value Wald=11.12 p=.001; interaction Wald=5.26 p=.022.
limits: Same limits as Expt 1. The interaction means the two factors are not additive.
agent_relevance: Strongest single data point against a pure-RCT trigger: a 12% knowledge-scope problem rose to 62% with a progress cue and no 'relax the constraint' step.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving, CogSci 42 - Discussion and RCT mechanism critique
finding: The authors say insight can occur with no constraint relaxation: after impasse, solvers search for moves that still look like progress, and solve when such a cue lies on the solution path. They say RCT does not explain how unwanted knowledge is switched off and back on, or how the right knowledge gets activated. They link CSP to Kaplan and Simon's detection of invariants and cite Ohlsson (2011) as a possible spreading-activation answer.
numbers: Method follows Knoblich et al 1999 Expt 1a: Roman-numeral pre-test (100 numbers, 5 min), then a 5-minute solve with the first idea written down (reminder at 30 s). Data are in a06 and a07.
quote: In our view, the mind's 'response to persistent failure' is not to try to forget what it knows; it is to try to find something better.
limits: Interpretation by a CSP-leaning group; RCT authors may disagree.
agent_relevance: Parsimony: an agent can get insight-like gains from a search rule (widen the move set when the progress check fails) without modelling mental constraints.

source: Ormerod, Rusconi, Banks & MacGregor (2015) Modelling insight: the case of the nine-dot problem, ICCM 2015
finding: ACT-R model of CSP for the nine-dot problem. Stage 1, maximisation: pick the line that cancels most dots, and accept it if cancelled dots exceed remaining dots divided by remaining lines. Otherwise mark it exhausted (criterion failure). Stage 2, relax minimisation: compare properties of failed moves (line length, angle, invariants) and extend the move space. Productions: P PROMISING, P EXHAUSTED, P COMPARE, P EXTEND.
numbers: 50 model runs: solution rate under 5% (humans: under 5%). 13-dot variant solved within 2 runs; 12- and 11-dot variants in under 10 runs. Inside-the-array first line needs fewer runs than an outside first line, p<.01, matching MacGregor 2001 Expts 4-5.
limits: Initial representation is hardwired. Whether maximising should be optimal or satisficing is untested. Only the nine-dot problem. Authors say knowledge-rich accounts may be overly elaborate here.
agent_relevance: A runnable insight trigger: criterion = remaining items / remaining budget; on failure, mine failed attempts for invariants and widen the action set. Fits S6 IMPASSE and G2.

source: Ormerod, MacGregor, Banks & Rusconi (2022) Conceptual recoding of new ideas during and after solution of an insight problem, CogSci 44
finding: A third account: idea discovery. After impasse, solvers compare their failed attempts, extract properties (angle, line length) and recode them as variables. They look first in the problem statement and their own attempts, and only later in memory or the environment. The 3-line nine-dot variant is easier than the 4-line, although it needs sharper angles and non-dot turns. The authors say neither RCT nor CSP predicts this directly.
numbers: N=136 (50 male, 86 female). Source problem: 3-line 24/69 (35%) vs 4-line 9/67 (12%). Logistic model chi2(3)=11.35, p=.01; Source Wald=7.63, p<.006; Array Wald=2.37, p=.124; interaction ns. 3-line source helped the 4-line transfer, not the reverse. Spaced dots helped overall.
limits: Between-subjects students, 10 attempts per sheet. The authors propose the theory in the same paper.
agent_relevance: Failed attempts are a priority source of new ideas. Feed the agent's own failed outputs (not the model's opinion) into the reframe step (G2).

source: Ormerod, Fioratou, Chronicle & MacGregor (2006) The remnants of insight, CogSci 28 - nine-dot evidence and re-solving
finding: Reports MacGregor 2001 Expts 4-5 as second-hand evidence. A first line that stays inside the array (diagonal) helps more than a line that goes outside (horizontal). That contradicts a pure knowledge or perceptual-block view, where an outside line should cue the solution, and fits progress monitoring (earlier criterion failure). The paper also says Jones (2003) and Kershaw and Ohlsson (2004) found both factors matter.
numbers: Solution rates 47% (diagonal) vs 28% (horizontal) in Expt 4 (134 participants); 65% vs 43% in Expt 5 (103). Weisberg and Alba 1981: 5 of 12 failed to solve the nine-dot problem 5 months after seeing the solution, and 8 of 23 failed after one week.
limits: MacGregor 2001 figures are second-hand. Authors are CSP proponents.
agent_relevance: Nice test of the hint: the 'obvious' knowledge cue (go outside) helped less than a progress cue. Trigger on failed progress, not on a knowledge hint alone.

source: Ormerod, Fioratou, Chronicle & MacGregor (2006) The remnants of insight - re-solving, necklace and 6-coin experiments
finding: Non-naive nine-dot solvers often remember 'go outside the array' but cannot rebuild the solution and revert to hill-climbing. The cheap-necklace hint ('destroy to create') did not help. A 6-coin variant arranged in a Y shape ('like a crab's claw') was solved at about the same rate as the standard layout at first, but re-solved much more often.
numbers: Of 40 non-naive nine-dot participants, 16 failed in two 30-s tries and 11 failed in 10 tries; of the 16, 13 made outside-the-array attempts. Necklace: standard solved by 1 hint and 2 control participants of 44; variant 5 hint and 6 control; all 44 re-solved the standard problem. 6-coin: standard 4 and Y-shape 6 solved first time (ns, N=34).
limits: Small samples. Failure to use a hint is also seen with shaded hints (Chronicle et al 2001).
agent_relevance: Knowing the insight is not enough. A reusable operator needs a single executable form (G3): store it as a runnable check or a named operation.

source: Ollinger, Fedor, Brodt & Szathmary (2017) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization, Psychological Research 81(5):925-938
finding: Hybrid test of both theories on a multi-step problem. Relaxing constraints alone (hint to use lines, or to use intersections) did not raise solution rate. Adding an explicit maximisation criterion (maximise intersections) did. Authors: relaxation is necessary but not sufficient; both are needed.
numbers: 119 analysed, about 30 per group. Solved: control 3/30 (10%); line hint 2/29 (7%); intersection hint 6/28 (21%); maximisation hint 21/29 (72%). Maximisation vs control chi2(1,59)=23.80, p<.0001, phi=.64; vs line group phi=.67; vs intersection group phi=.51. Before the hint, solvers used intersections more (47% vs 26% of non-solvers).
limits: One problem. Hint given at 5 min; 4 early solvers dropped. Authors favour hybrid models.
agent_relevance: Best direct support for 'both': reframe plus a search criterion beat reframe alone by about 3.4x (72% vs 21%). When the agent reframes, pair it with a computed progress measure on the new representation.

source: Ollinger, Fedor, Brodt & Szathmary (2017) ten-penny - solvers vs non-solvers
finding: Solvers showed promising moves earlier and had a higher maximisation and variation rate across attempts. Low variation (repeating one strategy) marked non-solvers. After hints almost everyone dropped the plain pennies strategy.
numbers: Participants using only the pennies strategy (variation zero) after 5 min: control 10 of 30 (33%); line 1/29 (3%); intersection 2/28 (7%); maximisation 0/29 (0%). Variation rate after hint F(3,115)=15.78, p<.001, partial eta2=.30.
limits: Same study; correlational for solvers vs non-solvers.
agent_relevance: Variation across attempts is a cheap code-measurable stuck signal: if consecutive attempts are near-identical, the impasse detector should fire (G1).

source: Graf, Danek, Vaci & Bilalic (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis, J Intelligence 11(5):86
finding: Eye tracking on a matchstick arithmetic problem (change an operator). ANOVA missed the shift, but GAMs and change-point analysis found an abrupt move of gaze from numbers to the key '+' sign at about 90% of solving time in solvers. After a hint, non-solvers refocused at once on operators and then faded; solvers shifted gradually.
numbers: Only 34% solved unaided; a further 11% after the hint 'You can change the operators, too.' Change point near the 90% time bin. After the hint, gaze on '=' doubled and on '+' rose about 4% at first, doubling by the 20% bin.
limits: One problem. Method paper. Sudden restructuring is visible only with nonlinear methods, so older null results may be method artefacts.
agent_relevance: Restructuring may be abrupt, so a trigger should be able to switch representation in one step, and a hint may give a burst that fades.

source: Spiridonov, Loginov, Ivanchei & Kurgansky (2019) The role of motor activity in insight problem solving (nine-dot), Frontiers in Psychology 10:2
finding: Finger drawing on a tablet, three experiments. Successful solvers moved more slowly and paused longer in the final third. The authors read this as off-line planning (lookahead), in line with MacGregor 2001. Practising non-dot turns of any angle raised solving a little. Practising the solution sequence in an unrelated task did not.
numbers: Pattern held in all three experiments; no single headline rate was recorded (tables not read).
limits: Motor measures; theory discussion short. The authors call both theories purely mental.
agent_relevance: Late-stage lookahead marks success. Allow extra deliberation at the impasse step only, and cap it elsewhere (G11).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo), arXiv 2509.14704
finding: 38 LLMs on 201 riddles built to need representational shift (puns, phonetic word play, kanji decomposition). Humans (n=126) scored 52.9%. Non-reasoning models averaged 7.6% and reasoning models 17.6%. The authors name RCT (constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition) as the target skill, but they do not test RCT against progress monitoring.
numbers: Human mean 10.58 of 20 (SD 7.11), 95% CI 46.6-59.2%. Reasoning vs non-reasoning: Welch t(24.093)=2.976, p=.00655, difference 9.8 points, 95% CI [3.0,16.6], d=0.946; pooled odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99-2.64). A later cut gives 9.4% and 19.3%. Only GPT-5 and some search-augmented models neared humans.
limits: One preprint, not independently replicated. Zero-shot only, no insight-specific prompting. Japanese items.
agent_relevance: On insight-style items reasoning models roughly double plain models yet stay far below humans. Extra thinking alone is not the trigger; see G11.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo - thought-log analysis (verification failure, language of thought)
finding: Models often wrote the right candidate in their reasoning but did not endorse it ('verification failure'), and rarely showed a reliable feeling of rightness. Thinking in Japanese did not help; some models did worse. The logs showed a stage pattern of impasse, trial and error, candidate evaluation, then verification.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-flash: about 15 log lines per question in English vs about 209 in Japanese, and 0 of 12 Japanese-thought answers correct. Grok-4: English thinking better, p=.0071. Claude-opus-4: no significant difference.
quote: models sometimes generated correct candidates but failed to endorse them
limits: Qualitative log reading, flagged by the authors as hypothesis generation. Logs may not reflect internal computation.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is endorsing the right answer, not generating it. This supports G5 and G8: an external check should select among candidates, not the model's own sense of rightness.

source: Qiu, Zhou & Schooler (2026) The cost of coordination: why multi-agent LLMs explore more but discover less, CogSci 48
finding: Solo GPT-4o vs unstructured two-agent GPT-4o teams on situation puzzles (insight, yes/no questions). Teams were less accurate although they explored more question categories and asked questions of equal quality. The deficit splits into 47% protocol failure (fewer questions to the host) and 53% residual, read as weak convergent integration.
numbers: N=82. Doubling time raised question volume in both (solo 179.9 to 374.8; team 49.2 to 95.9), keeping team about 26-27% of solo. Direct effect after mediators beta=-0.415, SE=0.146, p=.005. Total-question indirect effect -0.370, 95% BCa CI [-0.560,-0.183]; warmness indirect 0.010, ns.
limits: One model, one task type. The convergence reading rests on residual variance, as the authors say. It cites RCT but does not compare it with progress monitoring.
agent_relevance: More agents add breadth and cost convergence. Fits G9 and G4. Do not use agent talk as the insight trigger.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving, arXiv 2605.12970
finding: Human think-aloud study on new matchstick arithmetic problems (Knoblich and Ollinger paradigm), analysed with NLP. It reproduces the Knoblich difficulty order: loose-chunk value problems easiest, tautologies hardest. When the same transformation repeated, accuracy rose from 0.32 to 0.75 over five trials; with mixed types it stayed at 0.32-0.39.
numbers: N=189 (202 recruited, Prolific). 449/945 correct (47.5%); value-loose-chunk 80.7%, tautological 19.2%. After a first success: Same 83.7% vs Different 44.0% later correct; time 89.9 s vs 179.0 s. Trial x group beta=-0.524, p<.001; Different group lower overall beta=-0.747, p=.031.
limits: Human data. 4-minute limit. Does not pit RCT against progress monitoring.
agent_relevance: An independent replication of the chunk and tautology difficulty ordering on 25 new problems. A named, reusable 'type' label after a success is what transfers: store the recoded insight as a named operator.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) - speech signatures of restructuring
finding: On first-success trials people spoke more, talked about different things, and considered fewer candidate solutions. After the first success they kept changing how they spoke only when the same type recurred, and increasingly named the problem type.
numbers: Speech density higher on correct trials, beta=0.067, p=.009; this gap was smaller in the Different condition.
limits: Think-aloud may itself change the solving (Schooler et al 1993, cited in the source of a19).
agent_relevance: Fewer candidates plus naming the type marks a real restructure. Our log could use 'candidate count falls and a named operator appears' as a success marker.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey & Bhattacharya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a mental set? arXiv 2501.11833
finding: Einstellung-style test on mathematical equivalence problems with Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B and GPT-4o. In-context examples helped but did not change the number of steps. Zero-shot chain of thought raised accuracy and also step count, which the authors call a mental-set shift.
numbers: Six input problems per condition. GPT-4o few-shot exact match: shortcut 0.33; shortcut after complex-first 0.66; complex 0.66; complex after shortcut-first 0.83. Llama-70B: 0, 0.16, 0, 0.66. Llama-8B: 0.16, 0, 0, 0.
limits: Six items per cell gives no usable statistics. Not an insight paradigm. No theory comparison.
agent_relevance: Order and priming effects exist in LLMs, but this study is too small to set a trigger. Do not cite it as evidence.

source: Ollinger, Szathmary & Fedor (2023) Search and insight processes in card sorting games, Frontiers in Psychology 14:1118976
finding: A new insight paradigm built to probe RCT and search accounts. Available, salient perceptual features shaped the strategy people used. Discovering a non-obvious rule was hardest. People split between feature-integration and deliberate strategies for the same problem.
numbers: N=546 across two online experiments. No headline percentage extracted from this read.
limits: Abstract and discussion read; tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Individual strategy preferences mean one trigger will not fit every item class. A scaffold that mixes triggers by problem class fits.

source: Korovkin, Vladimirov, Chistopolskaya & Savinova (2018) How working memory provides representational change during insight problem solving, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Working-memory account of representational change. Full results were not read this session; only a keyword pass found that non-insight problems involve more progress monitoring, heuristics and operations in the problem space.
numbers: No numbers extracted.
limits: Opened only by keyword search, not read through; treat as a pointer.
agent_relevance: A pointer for angle B: working memory load may gate reframing.

source: Search note: LLM tests of the RCT vs progress-monitoring contrast
finding: No LLM study found that runs a head-to-head test of RCT and progress monitoring, or runs matchstick or nine-dot items with theory-specific predictions. The closest are NazoNazo (a17, a18), situation puzzles (a19) and mental set (a22).
numbers: Coverage: 4 WebSearch calls, Europe PMC and PubMed pages. The arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited, so coverage is partial.
limits: An absence claim for what this session could reach; not a proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence is missing, so trigger choice rests on human data. Plan our own test: reframe-only vs criterion-only vs both, at equal tokens (G7).
